claims.text: Wear performance of HEA protective coatings is governed primarily by microstructural homogeneity.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases and promoting a single-phase solid solution enhances coating toughness.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases and promoting a single-phase solid solution increases resistance to crack propagation under abrasive wear.
Changing substrate temperature or cooling rate can promote a more homogeneous single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
Changing substrate temperature or cooling rate can suppress intermetallic formation in an HEA coating.
The fraction of single-phase solid solution relative to intermetallic phases mediates wear performance.
Single-phase solid-solution microstructures distribute applied stress more evenly.
Single-phase solid-solution microstructures resist crack initiation and propagation.
Intermetallic phases act as brittle sites that facilitate crack growth.
Cracking associated with intermetallic phases facilitates material removal during wear.
A coating with a higher single-phase solid-solution fraction and fewer intermetallics will have a lower wear rate than a mixed-phase coating tested under identical conditions.
A coating with a higher single-phase solid-solution fraction and fewer intermetallics will resist material loss better than a coating with significant intermetallic content.
The proposed effect applies to HEA compositions capable of forming both single-phase and multiphase microstructures.
The proposed effect applies under abrasive conditions in which crack propagation is a dominant wear mechanism.
The hypothesis may not apply to compositions that inherently form only a single phase or only intermetallic phases.
The hypothesis may not apply when adhesive wear or high-temperature oxidation dominates wear.
